title: Prime Tally
statement: A lock designer wants to know how many prime numbers are available below a given size. Given the integer limit, return the count of prime numbers that are strictly less than limit. Recall that a prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.

examples.explanation: No prime is strictly less than 2.

hints.content: Testing each number by trial division works, but each test costs up to the square root of the number.
Instead of asking whether each number is prime, mark the numbers that are definitely not prime.
Every multiple of a prime p, starting from p × p, is composite.
Smaller multiples of p were already marked by smaller primes, which is why starting at p × p is enough.
Count the numbers that survive unmarked; each of them is prime.

testCases.explanation: No prime is strictly less than 2.
There are 1229 primes below 10000; trial division is noticeably slower here.

solutions.title: Trial division for each number
solutions.intuition: A number is composite exactly when some divisor no larger than its square root divides it.
solutions.approach: For every n below limit, test divisors from 2 up to the square root of n. Count the numbers with no divisor.
solutions.pseudocode: count = 0; for n from 2 to limit-1: if no d in [2, sqrt(n)] divides n then count++; return count.
commonMistakes: Testing divisors all the way to n instead of stopping at the square root.
Counting 1 as prime, or starting the loop at 0.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Trial division is easy to justify and fine for small limits. When many numbers must be classified at once, a sieve shares the work: each prime marks all of its multiples in one sweep instead of every number re-checking every divisor.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For limit 12, the numbers 2 and 3 have no divisor up to their square root.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10 have a small divisor; 5, 7 and 11 do not, giving 5 primes.

solutions.title: Sieve of composites
solutions.intuition: Rather than testing each number, let each prime cross out all of its multiples; whatever is never crossed out is prime.
solutions.approach: Allocate a flag per number. Walk upward; when a number is still unmarked, count it as prime and mark every multiple from its square onward. Multiples below the square were already marked by smaller primes.
solutions.pseudocode: flags = all false; for n from 2 to limit-1: if flags[n] is false then count++ and mark n*n, n*n+n, ... as composite; return count.
commonMistakes: Starting the marking at 2n instead of n×n, which still works but wastes time.
Allocating limit + 1 flags and accidentally counting limit itself.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I use a sieve: an array of flags where each unmarked number is prime and marks its multiples starting at its square. The total marking work is bounded by n log log n, far below trial division for large limits, at the cost of one byte per number. The strict inequality means I allocate exactly limit flags.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For limit 12, 2 is unmarked, so count it and mark 4, 6, 8 and 10.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: 3 is unmarked, so count it and mark 9. 4 is marked; 5 counts and its square 25 is beyond the limit.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: 7 and 11 are still unmarked and counted, for a total of 5.
